name: Ephesus
desc: Marble streets polished by two thousand years of feet run downhill from the Odeon to the Library of Celsus, whose two-storey façade still stands with its columns in place. The Great Theatre holds twenty-five thousand and the acoustics still work. The Terrace Houses, six Roman flats under a glass roof with frescoes and mosaic floors, are what most visitors skip.
season: Apr–May and Oct — July and August bake the marble and there is almost no shade
tip: Enter at the upper south gate and walk downhill to the lower gate, then take a taxi back to your car; doing it in reverse is an uphill slog in the heat.
todo: Terrace Houses under the glass roof
Library of Celsus façade at low sun
Curetes Street shopfronts and latrines
rev: Almost everyone calls it the best-preserved classical city they have walked, then complains about cruise-coach waves before noon and a ticket price that has climbed hard in three years.
entry: ≈€40 · Terrace Houses ≈€15 extra · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min by road to Selçuk, or the İZBAN suburban train to Selçuk and a 3 km taxi

name: Temple of Artemis
desc: One re-erected column with a stork's nest on top, standing in a marshy field of scattered drums and frog noise. That is all that survives of a building the ancients rated above the Pyramids. The anticlimax is the point: pace the foundation outline with Ayasuluk Hill and the İsa Bey Mosque lined up behind you.
season: Mar–May — the field floods after winter rain and the frogs take it over
tip: It is a five-minute walk from Selçuk's centre and free, so come at sunset when the mosque and castle behind it go gold and the coaches have left.
todo: Stand at the single standing column
Line up the Artemision, mosque and castle
Compare with the finds in Selçuk museum
rev: Visitors are split between those disappointed by a swamp with one column and those who find the emptiness moving; everyone agrees the roadside touts selling guidebooks are persistent.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min by road to Selçuk; it is signposted on the Selçuk–Ephesus road

name: Basilica of St John
desc: Justinian's six-domed basilica on Ayasuluk Hill was one of the largest churches in the world; now it is a cross-shaped field of re-erected columns and brick arches with a marble slab over the supposed tomb of the Evangelist. The hill also carries a Byzantine-Seljuk citadel and the best view over Selçuk's storks.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — exposed hilltop, no shade in high summer
tip: Buy the combined ticket that also covers the castle at the top of the hill, which many people walk past without realising it is open.
wiki: Basilica of Saint John the Theologian
todo: Marble tomb slab in the crossing
Baptistery pool beside the nave
Walk up to Ayasuluk castle
rev: Praised as quiet and uncrowded compared with Ephesus, though several note that the reconstruction is heavy-handed and the interpretation boards are faded to illegibility.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min by road or İZBAN train to Selçuk; the hill is a 10-min walk from the station

name: House of the Virgin Mary
desc: A small stone chapel in pine forest on Bülbül Dağı, identified from the visions of a German nun and endorsed by three popes. Inside it is dim, candle-smelling and takes about ninety seconds to walk through. Outside, a wall of paper prayer slips tied by Muslims and Christians alike is the more interesting sight.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — cool under the pines even when Selçuk is at 38 °C
tip: Arrive before 09:00 or after 16:00; between those hours the Kuşadası cruise coaches queue the chapel entrance forty deep.
todo: The prayer-slip wall below the chapel
Drink from the three spring taps
Look back down over the Küçük Menderes plain
rev: Pilgrims find it genuinely affecting; secular visitors often report a two-minute chapel, a stiff entry fee, a car-park charge on top and an aggressive gift shop.
entry: ≈₺600 (≈€14) plus a vehicle charge · not covered by the Museum Pass
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then to Selçuk and 7 km of hairpins up Bülbül Dağı; taxis wait at the Ephesus lower gate

name: Şirince
desc: A Greek-built hill village of whitewashed stone houses with wooden overhangs, emptied in the 1923 exchange and refilled by tourism. Two abandoned churches, cobbled lanes too steep for cars, and vineyards on every slope. The fruit wine is mostly sugar and marketing; the olive oil, dried figs and village breakfast are the real reason to come.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — weekends are gridlocked from May onward
tip: Park in the lower lot and walk up; the top of the village past St John the Baptist church empties out completely and has the terrace views everyone photographs from below.
todo: St Demetrius church at the top of the lane
Village breakfast with local olives
Olive-oil soap from a workshop, not a stall
rev: People love the stone lanes and the breakfast, and are near-unanimous that the fruit-wine hard sell and the wall-to-wall souvenir stalls on the main street have gone too far.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then Selçuk and 8 km of switchbacks east; minibuses run from Selçuk otogar roughly hourly

name: Çamlık Railway Museum
desc: Thirty-odd steam locomotives parked on open track in a pine hollow south of Selçuk, most of them British and German engines that worked the Ottoman lines. You can climb into cabs, walk the turntable and go through a short tunnel with a preserved train inside. Rust, oil smell and cicadas, almost no supervision.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the metal is untouchable in August sun
tip: Bring a torch: the tunnel section with the sleeping-car set is unlit and most people turn back at the entrance without seeing it.
todo: Climb into a Prussian G8 cab
Walk the turntable pit
The dark tunnel with the carriage set
rev: Rail enthusiasts rate it one of the best open collections in the eastern Mediterranean; others report peeling paint, no English labelling and a café that is often shut.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then Selçuk and 10 km south on the Aydın road; Çamlık is signposted off the D550

name: Kemeraltı Bazaar
desc: A living Ottoman bazaar following the curve of a filled-in harbour: coppersmiths, spice sacks, thirty hans, a working synagogue quarter and coffee served in courtyards under vine. It is not curated for tourists, which is why it works. Kızlarağası Han and the Havra Sokağı fish and pickle street are the two poles.
season: Year-round — best Oct–May; the covered lanes trap heat in August
tip: Go on a weekday morning and enter through Havra Sokağı from Anafartalar Caddesi; the tourist end near Konak is the least interesting part of the whole bazaar.
todo: Coffee in Kızlarağası Han courtyard
Havra Sokağı fish and pickle stalls
Şadırvanaltı and Hisar mosques
rev: Repeatedly called the most authentic bazaar in Türkiye after Istanbul's, with the caveats that it is genuinely confusing to navigate, several hans are half-derelict, and pickpocketing near Konak is real.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN train to Konak and walk 300 m inland; the metro stop is Çankaya

name: Kadifekale
desc: The acropolis of Smyrna, founded by Alexander's generals, sits on a bare hill 180 m above the gulf. The walls are Hellenistic below and Byzantine-Ottoman above, and there is a huge Roman cistern inside. What people come for is the view: the whole horseshoe of İzmir, the bay and the ferries laid out at once.
season: Year-round — go at sunset any month; the hilltop is windy and exposed
tip: Take the 33 bus from Konak rather than walking up through the neighbourhood, and come down before dark — the streets below are poor and unlit.
todo: Sunset over the gulf from the west wall
Roman cistern inside the enceinte
Tea from the hilltop çay bahçesi
rev: The panorama is universally rated the best in İzmir, but visitors consistently flag litter inside the walls, ongoing excavation fencing and a run-down approach that puts some people off.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then metro to Konak and the 33 city bus up the hill; taxis from Konak take 10 min

name: Agora of Smyrna
desc: A Roman civic square rebuilt by Marcus Aurelius after the earthquake of 178, sunk two storeys below the modern street grid. The basement galleries are the surprise: rows of vaulted arches, still carrying water in their original channels, with graffiti scratched by second-century citizens. Apartment blocks lean over the whole thing.
season: Oct–May — the sunken court holds heat badly in July and August
tip: Go down into the west basilica vaults rather than staying on the upper court; the Roman graffiti and the working water channel are down there and are easy to miss entirely.
todo: Vaulted basement galleries
Ancient graffiti on the vault walls
Corinthian colonnade on the north stoa
rev: Praised as an unexpected, near-empty Roman site inside a working city; complaints centre on patchy signage, closed sections behind excavation fencing and the rubbish blown in from the streets above.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then metro to Çankaya and a 10-min walk uphill through Kemeraltı's back lanes

name: Asansör (Historical Elevator)
desc: A brick lift tower built in 1907 by the Jewish banker Nesim Levi so residents of the Karataş cliff would not have to climb 155 steps. The cabin still runs, free, up 51 metres to a terrace restaurant over the gulf. Below it, Dario Moreno Street is a lane of restored Levantine houses in ochre and pink.
season: Year-round — the terrace is best an hour before sunset
tip: Walk up Dario Moreno Sokak first and take the lift down, then have the sunset drink at the terrace bar rather than paying for the restaurant dinner.
todo: Ride the original lift shaft
Dario Moreno Sokak's painted houses
Sunset over the gulf from the terrace
rev: Locals and visitors both like the free ride and the view; the recurring gripe is that the terrace restaurant charges tourist prices for mediocre food and the queue at sunset can run twenty minutes.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN to Konak and the 169 bus or a 20-min walk south along the shore

name: Alsancak and the Kordon
desc: İzmir's Levantine quarter: grid streets of tall shuttered houses behind a two-kilometre grass waterfront where the whole city sits at dusk with beer and sunflower seeds. Horse carriages have gone, phaeton stands remain. Kıbrıs Şehitleri and the narrow bar lanes off it are where İzmir actually drinks and eats.
season: Year-round — Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct are ideal; the Kordon is windy and grey in January
tip: Cross to the Karşıyaka side on the municipal ferry at sunset for about a euro — it is the cheapest and best boat trip in the city and locals use it as a commute.
todo: Sunset ferry to Karşıyaka
Boyoz and gevrek at a Kordon kiosk
Bar lanes off Kıbrıs Şehitleri Caddesi
rev: Consistently described as the most relaxed big-city waterfront in Türkiye, with complaints about weekend noise from the bars, thin parking and gulf water that smells in still August weather.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN suburban train straight to Alsancak station in about 25 min

name: Basmane Station
desc: The 1866 terminus of the Ottoman line to Aydın, a low stone building with a cast-iron train shed and a clock that still keeps time. Trains to Denizli and Selçuk leave from platforms that look unchanged since the 1930s. The quarter around it — cheap hotels, tea houses, Syrian bakeries — is the unpolished counterweight to Alsancak.
season: Year-round — the district is livelier and safer in daylight
tip: Take the regional train from here to Selçuk instead of the coach: it costs almost nothing, runs along the Küçük Menderes plain and drops you a walk from the Artemision.
todo: Cast-iron train shed from platform 1
Regional train to Selçuk or Ödemiş
Breakfast in the Basmane tea gardens
rev: Rail travellers appreciate the intact Victorian shed and cheap regional fares; the surrounding streets get repeated warnings for after-dark hustle, and services are cut without notice during track works.
entry: Free to enter · regional tickets a few euros
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN to Basmane, which is also the metro interchange for the old city

name: Gediz Delta Bird Paradise
desc: Twenty minutes from downtown İzmir the city stops and forty thousand hectares of salt pans, lagoons and reedbed begin. Around ten thousand flamingos breed here on a purpose-built island, the largest colony in Türkiye, and pelicans, avocets and marsh harriers work the shallows. Flat gravel tracks, hides, and no crowds at all.
season: Nov–Apr for numbers, Jun–Jul for flamingo chicks — Aug is hot, still and mosquito-heavy
tip: Bring your own binoculars and go early: the hides face east, so morning light is behind you and the salt-pan haze has not started.
todo: Flamingo island from the main hide
Cycle the salt-pan dykes
Dalmatian pelicans in winter
rev: Birders rate it world-class for flamingos, while casual visitors often leave disappointed: the birds are distant without a scope, the access road is rough and parts close during the breeding season.
entry: Free — the adjoining Doğal Yaşam Parkı charges separately
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN to Çiğli and a taxi to Sasalı; a car is realistically necessary for the dyke tracks

name: Mount Yamanlar and Karagöl
desc: The pine mountain behind Karşıyaka, with a small dark crater-shaped lake in a fold near the top that İzmir families have picnicked at for a century. Legend hangs Tantalus on it. From the ridge you look down on the whole gulf on one side and the Gediz plain on the other, with nothing between you and the wind.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — snow is possible in January, and summer weekends are picnic chaos
tip: Go on a weekday: on Sundays the single-lane road up is nose-to-tail and the lake shore disappears under barbecue smoke.
todo: Walk the loop around Karagöl
Ridge viewpoint over the gulf
Grilled köfte at a forest lokanta
rev: Locals value it as the nearest real forest to the city; visitors coming for the lake often say it is smaller and more littered than the photographs suggest, and the road has some rough sections.
entry: Free · small parking charge at the lake
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then İZBAN to Karşıyaka and 40 min by car up the forest road; buses are infrequent

name: Çeşme
desc: The tip of the peninsula facing Chios, with a Genoese castle over the harbour and a chain of coves running south to Pırlanta and Altınkum. The water is startlingly clear and colder than the rest of the Aegean because of the meltemi. Out of season it reverts to a quiet fishing and thermal town.
season: Jun and Sep are ideal — July and August are gridlocked and the meltemi can blow for a week
tip: Skip the town beaches and drive 8 km south to Altınkum's string of small sandy coves; the last one along has no music and a shack selling grilled fish.
todo: Altınkum's southern coves
Ferry across to Chios for the day
Sakız tatlısı at a harbour café
rev: Reliably clear water and good day-trips to Chios, offset by İstanbul-level summer prices, a motorway that jams solid on Friday afternoons and a wind that can shut the beaches down.
entry: Free · beach clubs charge ₺500–1,500 for a lounger in season
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 80 min west on the O-32 motorway; frequent coaches from İzmir Üçkuyular otogar

name: Çeşme Castle
desc: A squat Genoese fortress rebuilt by Bayezid II in 1508, sitting directly above the ferry quay with a dry moat and six towers you can walk. Inside is a small archaeological museum and a room on the 1770 naval battle of Çeşme, when the Russian fleet burned the Ottoman one in the strait you are looking at.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the ramparts are shadeless at midday
tip: Climb the seaward tower late in the afternoon when the Chios ferry comes in; the castle closes earlier than the harbour bars suggest, usually around 17:00 out of season.
todo: Walk the full rampart circuit
Naval battle of Çeşme room
Amphorae in the courtyard museum
rev: A quick, cheap and genuinely well-preserved fort with harbour views; the museum inside is thin, the labelling minimal, and in July the courtyard is an oven.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 80 min west on the O-32; the castle is above the ferry terminal in the town centre

name: Alaçatı
desc: A Greek stone village of blue shutters and bougainvillea that became Türkiye's most photographed small town, plus a shallow bay four kilometres south with reliable side-shore wind that is one of the best windsurf and kite spots in Europe. Old stone windmills line the ridge. Mastic, herbs and sea beans on every menu.
season: May–Jun and Sep for wind and space — August is expensive and shoulder-to-shoulder
tip: Sleep in the village but eat in Alaçatı's back lanes rather than Kemalpaşa Caddesi, and check the wind forecast — the same meltemi that makes the bay perfect makes the beaches unusable.
todo: Windsurf the waist-deep bay
Saturday herb and produce market
Stone windmills at sunset
rev: The stone streets and the windsurf bay both live up to the hype; the near-universal complaint is that prices are the highest on the Aegean and the village is now more boutique hotel than village.
entry: Free · windsurf board and wetsuit hire ≈€40–60 a day
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 70 min on the O-32; the bay is a further 10 min south by road from the village

name: Ilıca Beach
desc: A long shallow bay of pale sand where hot springs bubble up through the seabed, so the water in places is noticeably warmer than the rest of the peninsula. You can wade a hundred metres and still be waist-deep, which makes it the family beach of the Çeşme coast. Thermal hotels line the back of the sand.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the public end is packed solid through August
tip: Walk to the far eastern end past the last hotel to find where the hot springs actually vent — you feel the warm patches with your feet and almost nobody swims there.
todo: Find the warm spring patches offshore
Thermal hamam at a spa hotel
Sunset walk the full length of the sand
rev: Parents rate the shallow warm water highly; the standard complaints are the crowds, the wall of hotel loungers blocking access and seaweed in still weather.
entry: Free at the public section · beach clubs ₺400–1,000
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 75 min on the O-32; Ilıca is 5 km before Çeşme town and served by the same coaches

name: Erythrae
desc: One of the twelve Ionian cities, spread over a hill above the fishing village of Ildır with its theatre cut into the slope and city walls running through olive terraces. Sheep graze the orchestra. The bay below is scattered with islets and the water off the ancient harbour is shallow enough to see submerged walls.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the hill is unshaded and hot from July
tip: The site is unfenced and free; park in Ildır village by the harbour and walk up the track past the mosque rather than trying to drive the last stretch.
todo: Theatre seats in the hillside
Submerged harbour walls in the shallows
Fish lunch at Ildır harbour
rev: Visitors love having a whole Ionian city to themselves with a sea view, but note that there is essentially no signage, the paths are goat tracks and the museum finds have all gone to İzmir.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then the O-32 to Çeşme and 20 km north-east on a small road to Ildır village

name: Karaburun Peninsula
desc: A long empty finger of limestone north of Çeşme with almost no development: narcissus fields in winter, wild olive, goat herds and a corniche road that hangs over the sea for forty kilometres. Coves like Ardıç and Denizgiren are reached down dirt tracks. Monk seals still use the caves on the western cliffs.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter narcissus in Jan–Feb, but many places shut Nov–Mar
tip: Drive the western coast road from Mordoğan to Sarpıncık lighthouse in the late afternoon and carry water and fuel — there is one petrol station on the whole peninsula.
todo: Sarpıncık lighthouse road at sunset
Swim at Ardıç or Denizgiren cove
Buy peninsula olive oil and narcissus honey
rev: Consistently described as the emptiest coast within reach of a major Turkish city; the trade-offs are potholed side tracks, thin phone signal and restaurants that close entirely out of season.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h north-west via Urla and Mordoğan; there is no realistic public transport beyond Mordoğan

name: Mordoğan
desc: The only real town on the Karaburun peninsula's east coast, a strip of low houses facing the gulf with Foça visible across the water. Small pebble beaches, a fishing harbour, one street of shops and a promenade where the whole town walks at dusk. Almond and tangerine groves come right down to the shore.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct are the pleasant quiet months
tip: Buy the local almonds and mandarins directly from the roadside stands north of town rather than in the shops, and eat at the harbour fish restaurants where the boats tie up.
todo: Fish dinner at the harbour
Swim off the pebble coves north of town
Roadside almond and mandarin stalls
rev: Regulars value it as an unglamorous, affordable alternative to Çeşme; newcomers sometimes find it plain, with narrow stony beaches and a summer weekend traffic crush on the single access road.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 90 min via Urla and the peninsula road; minibuses run from İzmir Üçkuyular otogar

name: Foça
desc: Ancient Phokaia, the city that founded Marseille, now a low harbour town of stone houses in two bays split by a Genoese castle wall. Fishing boats, a seafront of meyhanes, and offshore the Siren Rocks, a protected reserve where one of the last Mediterranean monk seal populations breeds in sea caves.
season: May–Jun and Sep — August fills with İzmir weekenders and prices double
tip: Take a boat tour that circles the Siren Islands rather than one that lands on them; the seal caves are closed to landing and the operators who promise otherwise are the ones to avoid.
todo: Boat trip round the Siren Rocks
Fish meze on the small harbour
Taş Ev and the Persian rock tomb
rev: People come back for the harbour atmosphere and the seal-watching chance, while noting that actually seeing a monk seal is rare, the town beaches are small, and summer weekend parking is hopeless.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 70 min north on the O-33 and the Menemen road; regular coaches from İzmir otogar

name: Yenifoça
desc: Old Foça's quieter twin twenty kilometres up the coast: a Genoese-era grid of stone houses with carved doorframes, a tiny harbour and a shoreline of flat rock slabs people swim off. Almost no hotels, a handful of pensions in restored houses, and a coast road north past deserted bays toward the wind farms.
season: Jun–Sep for the water; Apr–May and Oct for the village with nobody in it
tip: Swim from the rock shelves north of the harbour instead of the small town beach, and eat at a village lokanta rather than the seafront — the seafront is priced for the weekenders.
todo: Carved stone doorframes in the back lanes
Swim off the flat rock shelves
Coast road north to the empty bays
rev: Described as what Foça was twenty years ago, with the caveats that there is little to do beyond swim and eat, most places shut from November, and the sea is weedy in still weather.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 80 min north via Menemen and Foça; minibuses connect from Foça in about 25 min

name: Urla
desc: A market town on the peninsula that has become the centre of Türkiye's Aegean wine and food revival: a dozen boutique wineries along the Urla Bağ Yolu, an artichoke festival in April, and a restored Greek quarter of art shops on Necati Bey Caddesi. Urla İskele down at the water is where the seafood is.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the artichoke festival is early April, harvest events in September
tip: Book winery visits in advance and hire a driver; the Bağ Yolu is a proper tasting route with six or seven producers and no public transport whatsoever.
todo: Taste Bornova Misketi on the Bağ Yolu
Artichoke dishes at Urla İskele
Art street in the old Greek quarter
rev: The wine route and the seafood get genuine praise, though visitors regularly report İstanbul prices, wineries that turn away walk-ins, and a town centre that is now more concept store than market.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 45 min west on the O-32; İZBAN does not reach Urla, so a car is the practical option

name: Klazomenai
desc: An Ionian city on the Urla shore whose great find is a sixth-century BC olive oil workshop, reconstructed and working: the crushing stone, the settling tanks and the lever press have been rebuilt so you can see how classical oil was actually made. The rest of the site is low walls, mosaics and a causeway to Karantina Island.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — flat, exposed and hot at midday in summer
tip: Combine it with the causeway walk to Karantina Island, the 1860s Ottoman quarantine station, which is restored and open and almost nobody joins the two visits up.
todo: Reconstructed Archaic olive oil press
Causeway to Karantina Island
Anaxagoras memorial in Urla
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find the working oil workshop genuinely unusual; others report a small, dusty site with limited English signage and irregular opening hours out of season.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 45 min west on the O-32 to Urla and 4 km down to İskele

name: Sığacık
desc: A village built inside a 16th-century Ottoman fortress, with houses using the curtain wall as their back wall and lanes barely wide enough for a handcart. A marina sits outside the gate and a Sunday producers' market fills the castle square with village women selling herbs, cheese and sea beans.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the Sunday market runs year-round, the marina empties in winter
tip: Come on a Sunday morning for the market inside the walls, then walk the two kilometres to Akkum beach rather than driving into the marina car park.
todo: Sunday producers' market in the castle
Walk the full circuit of the walls
Boat out to the Teos coves
rev: The castle village and the market are widely liked; complaints focus on the marina development changing the feel, tight parking and restaurants that have raised prices well past the village's means.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min south-west via Seferihisar; minibuses run from Seferihisar centre

name: Teos
desc: The birthplace of Anacreon and the headquarters of the Dionysian actors' guild, set in olive groves a kilometre from the sea. The Temple of Dionysos has been substantially re-erected in recent seasons and its columns now stand again among the trees. There is also a theatre, a bouleuterion and two silted harbours.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the grove gives some shade but July heat is heavy
tip: Walk on past the temple to the south harbour, a quiet sandy inlet where the ancient mole is still visible underwater and you can swim after the site visit.
todo: Re-erected Temple of Dionysos
Theatre hollow above the plain
Swim at the silted south harbour
rev: The re-erected temple among olive trees is called the loveliest small site on this coast; the site is unfenced, unstaffed and unsigned, so visitors without a guidebook often miss half of it.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min to Seferihisar and 5 km down the Sığacık road; signposted from the village

name: Seferihisar
desc: Türkiye's first Cittaslow town, which in practice means tangerine groves, a seed-exchange market, restored village houses in Ulamış and Düzce, and a deliberate refusal of the apartment blocks that ate the rest of the coast. Doğanbey, an abandoned Greek hill village above the town, is being slowly repaired house by house.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the mandarin harvest and its festival fall in December
tip: Drive up to Doğanbey village in the late afternoon: it is empty apart from a couple of cafés, the light on the stone is extraordinary, and there is no sign from the main road.
todo: Doğanbey hill village at golden hour
Cittaslow producers' market
Mandarin groves and December festival
rev: Praised for keeping its shape while its neighbours built high, though several visitors say the Cittaslow branding is thicker than the substance and the town centre itself is unremarkable.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 45 min south-west on the Seferihisar road; frequent minibuses from Üçkuyular

name: Gümüldür and the Menderes coast
desc: The stretch of shore between Özdere and Ahmetbeyli, backed by tangerine orchards that scent the whole coast road in December. Long sand-and-shingle beaches, unfashionable family pensions, and the ancient sites of Claros and Notion within a few kilometres. This is where İzmir families rent a summer flat rather than a boutique hotel.
season: Jun–Sep for the sea; December for the mandarin harvest and empty beaches
tip: Buy mandarins straight from the orchard gates on the Gümüldür–Ahmetbeyli road; the roadside stalls nearer the beach charge triple for the same fruit.
todo: Swim the long Özdere sand
Orchard-gate mandarins in winter
Combine with Claros and Notion
rev: Turkish families rate it good value with clean shallow water; foreign visitors often find it a scrappy strip of concrete holiday blocks, and the summer traffic on the single coast road is heavy.
entry: Free · beach clubs charge modestly by Çeşme standards
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 45 min south on the coast road via Gümüldür; minibuses run from Üçkuyular otogar

name: Claros
desc: The oracle of Apollo that rivalled Delphi, sitting in a waterlogged hollow behind the beach at Ahmetbeyli. Enormous drums of the temple's Doric columns lie where the earthquakes dropped them, half in standing water, and colossal marble feet from the cult statues survive. Below the temple are the vaulted rooms where prophecies were delivered.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the hollow floods in winter and mosquitoes own it in high summer
tip: Wear boots you do not mind soaking: the site sits below the water table and the walkways are frequently submerged, which is exactly why so few people bother with it.
todo: Colossal marble feet of Apollo
Fallen Doric drums in the water
Sacred way and its statue bases
rev: Those who make it call it one of the most atmospheric sites in Ionia, with the standard caveats: standing water, biting insects, minimal signage and an entrance that is often unstaffed.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min south to Ahmetbeyli; the site is signposted 1 km inland from the coast road

name: Pergamon
desc: An acropolis stacked on a 300-metre crag, with the steepest theatre of the ancient world — eighty rows dropping almost vertically into the valley. The library rivalled Alexandria and gave us parchment. The Great Altar's terrace is empty because the frieze is in Berlin, which locals will tell you about within the first minute.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the crag is fully exposed and July tops 38 °C
tip: Take the cable car up but walk down the ancient road past the Temple of Demeter and the gymnasium terraces; the descent is the half of the site the coaches never see.
todo: Stand at the top of the vertical theatre
Empty terrace of the Great Altar
Trajaneum's white marble colonnade
rev: The theatre and the setting draw superlatives; complaints are about the cable-car queue at midday, the missing altar frieze, and vertigo on the theatre steps, which have no handrail.
entry: ≈₺900 (≈€20) plus cable car ≈₺200 · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h north on the O-33 and D550 to Bergama; coaches run from İzmir otogar hourly

name: Asklepion of Pergamon
desc: The Roman world's most famous healing sanctuary, where Galen trained: a colonnaded sacred way, a theatre for patient therapy, sacred springs, and a vaulted tunnel down which attendants whispered suggestions to sleeping patients on their way to the round treatment temple. Dream interpretation, mud baths and music were the prescriptions.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — flat, shadeless and hot from July
tip: Walk the underground tunnel slowly and listen; the acoustics and the light shafts are the whole point, and most groups march through it in twenty seconds.
todo: The whispering treatment tunnel
Drink from the sacred spring
Theatre used as patient therapy
rev: The tunnel and the sacred way impress most visitors, though several note that the site sits inside a military zone with photography restrictions at the gate and that separate tickets from the acropolis add up.
entry: ≈₺500 (≈€11) · separate from the acropolis · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h north to Bergama; the sanctuary is 3 km west of the town centre by taxi

name: Red Basilica
desc: A colossal red-brick temple to the Egyptian gods, built by Hadrian, straddling the Selinus river on two tunnels that still carry the water. One of the round side towers has been rebuilt as a mosque and is in use. Inside the main hall the brick walls rise nineteen metres and swallows nest in the arcades.
season: Year-round — spring and autumn best; the brick hall stays cool even in July
tip: Walk down to the riverbank behind the building to see the two vaulted tunnels the whole temple is built over — almost nobody goes round the back.
todo: Brick nave and its swallow colonies
Vaulted river tunnels underneath
Rebuilt south tower, now a mosque
rev: The sheer scale of the brickwork surprises people; the usual grumbles are scaffolding that has been up for years, restricted access to the towers and an entry fee for a building you see in twenty minutes.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h north to Bergama; the basilica is in the old town, walkable from the bazaar

name: Allianoi
desc: A Roman thermal spa town north of Bergama, with baths still fed by a 45 °C spring and an intact vaulted bathing hall, deliberately buried under sand and flooded by the Yortanlı dam in 2011 after a decade of legal fights. The bridge and the hot spring outflow remain visible at the reservoir edge in dry years.
season: Aug–Oct when the reservoir is at its lowest and more of the site is exposed
tip: Ask at the Bergama museum first — what you can actually see depends entirely on the year's water level, and in a wet spring there is nothing above the surface at all.
todo: Roman bridge at the reservoir edge
Thermal spring outflow
Allianoi finds in Bergama museum
rev: Visitors describe it as a site to mourn rather than tour: usually nothing but water and a bridge, no facilities, no signage, and a story that Turkish archaeologists still consider a scandal.
entry: Free — there is no ticketed site left to enter
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h to Bergama and 18 km north-east toward Paşaköy on a minor road

name: Mount Nif and the Karabel Relief
desc: Above Kemalpaşa, on the old pass road, a life-size Hittite warrior is carved into a rock face — spear, bow, curved sword, hieroglyphs — the figure Herodotus mistook for an Egyptian pharaoh. The mountain behind holds a Lydian fortress, Byzantine ruins and cherry orchards that supply half of İzmir in June.
season: Apr–Jun for cherries and green slopes, Sep–Oct for clear air; the pass road is grim in winter rain
tip: The relief is in a damp gully off the Kemalpaşa–Torbalı road with one small brown sign; park at the layby and walk down, and go in the morning when light reaches into the cleft.
todo: Karabel Hittite warrior relief
Kemalpaşa cherries in June
Ottoman Nymphaion palace ruins
rev: Hittite enthusiasts think it worth the detour, but most visitors report a weathered, graffiti-scratched carving behind a rusty grille, poor signposting and nowhere sensible to park.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 35 min east to Kemalpaşa; the relief is 20 km further on the Torbalı road

name: Bayındır
desc: The flower town of the Küçük Menderes valley: greenhouses and open fields of carnations, roses and seasonal cut flowers supply markets across Türkiye, and in April the roadsides are solid colour. The old centre has Ottoman houses, a covered market and a çarşı where the flower auction happens early and loudly.
season: Apr–May for the flower fields and the festival; the rest of the year it is a working farm town
tip: Be at the flower market by 07:00 — the auction is over by mid-morning and by lunchtime the town is just another Aegean market centre.
todo: Early-morning flower auction
Carnation fields in April
Ottoman houses around the old çarşı
rev: Visitors who time the April flower festival right find it genuinely colourful; outside those weeks people describe an ordinary agricultural town with little to detain them.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 55 min south-east via Torbalı; regional trains from Basmane also stop here

name: Ödemiş
desc: The market town under Bozdağ, with a Wednesday bazaar that pulls in the whole Küçük Menderes valley and a private ethnographic museum, the Yıldız Kent Arşivi, that is far better than a town this size deserves. Potatoes, chestnuts and the local kestane şekeri are the produce; Birgi is fifteen minutes away.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the valley floor is 38 °C in July and August
tip: Come on a Wednesday for the bazaar and take the old regional train from İzmir Basmane rather than driving; it is slow, cheap and runs through the whole valley.
todo: Wednesday bazaar in the old çarşı
Ödemiş Museum's Ottoman collection
Chestnut candy from a town confectioner
rev: Useful as a base for Birgi and Bozdağ and liked for the bazaar, though most visitors agree the town itself is plain concrete and there is little reason to stay a second night.
entry: Free · town museum a few euros
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 20 by road via Torbalı, or the regional train from İzmir Basmane in about 2 h

name: Birgi
desc: The Aydınid capital, a village of timber-framed houses with painted ceilings stepping up a wooded slope, and at its heart the 1312 Great Mosque with a carved walnut minbar and a mihrab of Seljuk tiles. The Çakırağa Mansion has murals of Istanbul and Venice painted by someone who had never seen either.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the mosque and mansion close for lunch, and August is airless
tip: Check whether Çakırağa Mansion is open before you drive up; it has been closed for restoration in stretches and it is the single best interior in the village.
todo: Walnut minbar in the Great Mosque
Çakırağa Mansion wall paintings
Plane tree and coffee at the meydan
rev: Widely called the best-preserved Ottoman village in the Aegean interior, with recurring complaints about erratic opening hours, restoration scaffolding and weekend coach parties from İzmir.
entry: Small fee — check locally · mosque free
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 30 via Ödemiş; frequent minibuses cover the last 9 km from Ödemiş

name: Bozdağ
desc: A chestnut-forest village at 1,150 m on the ridge above Ödemiş, with İzmir's only ski centre on the slopes above and cold spring water everywhere. In winter there are five lifts and reliable snow; in summer it is where the valley escapes the heat, and the road over the top to Gölcük is one of the best drives in the province.
season: Jan–Mar for skiing, Jun–Sep for the cool air and chestnut woods
tip: The ski centre is small and gets İzmir day-trippers on weekends; go midweek, and in summer drive the ridge road towards Gölcük for the views back down over the plain.
todo: Ski or sledge the ridge slopes
Chestnut woods above the village
Ridge road to Gölcük lake
rev: Locals are fond of it as a cheap, close ski hill, but experienced skiers call the runs short and the lift infrastructure dated, and the access road ices over badly after dark.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 via Ödemiş and 25 km of switchbacks; winter tyres are needed Dec–Mar

name: Gölcük Lake
desc: A small crater-shaped lake at 1,000 m in the Bozdağ range, ringed by pine and chestnut and reflecting the ridge on still mornings. There is a walking loop of about three kilometres, a handful of wooden restaurants serving trout and gözleme, and mist that sits on the water until mid-morning in autumn.
season: May–Oct — beautiful under snow in winter but the last kilometres often need chains
tip: Walk the far side of the loop, away from the restaurants; that is where the reflections are and where the picnic crowd never goes.
todo: Loop walk round the lake shore
Trout and gözleme at a wooden lokanta
Autumn mist at first light
rev: A reliable escape from the valley heat and popular with İzmir families; on summer weekends the shore is wall-to-wall barbecues and litter, and the lake level drops noticeably by September.
entry: Free · small parking charge in season
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 via Ödemiş and the Bozdağ road; no public transport to the lake itself

name: Tire
desc: An old Aydınid and Ottoman trade town with more than twenty surviving mosques, several hans and a Tuesday market that is one of the largest in the Aegean. The town still makes felt, keçe carpets and camel-hair goods by hand, and the local dish, Tire köftesi, is worth the drive on its own.
season: Year-round; the Tuesday market is the reason to time it — avoid midsummer midday heat
tip: Find one of the two remaining felt workshops behind the bazaar and watch keçe being beaten; ask at the Yeşil İmaret mosque and someone will point you.
todo: Tuesday market across the whole town
Watch felt being made by hand
Tire köftesi at a bazaar lokanta
rev: Food-minded travellers rate the market and the köfte highly; others find the monuments scattered, poorly signed and often locked outside prayer times, with little in English anywhere.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h south-east via Torbalı; regional trains from Basmane stop at Tire

name: Sardis
desc: Croesus's capital, where coinage was invented. Two sites a kilometre apart: a marble gymnasium façade re-erected to full height beside the largest ancient synagogue known, its floor a carpet of mosaic; and up a gorge, the Temple of Artemis with two enormous standing columns under crumbling badland cliffs.
season: Apr–May and Oct — the Gediz plain is punishing in July and August
tip: Do both parts: many visitors stop at the roadside gymnasium and never drive the extra kilometre up to the temple, which is the better of the two.
todo: Re-erected marble court of the gymnasium
Mosaic floor of the great synagogue
Two standing columns at the Artemis temple
rev: The synagogue mosaics and the gymnasium façade draw real admiration; the frequent complaints are the highway noise beside the site, two separate entrance points and almost no shade or facilities.
entry: ≈₺300 (≈€7) covering both sections · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 east via Turgutlu and Salihli; trains from İzmir Basmane stop at Sart

name: Sart
desc: The village that grew on top of Sardis, where Roman column drums serve as garden walls and the Pactolus stream — the one whose gold made Croesus rich — runs behind the houses. Vineyards for sultana raisins stretch to the horizon and roadside stalls sell them by the kilo from August onward.
season: Sep–Oct for the grape harvest; Apr–May for green hills and wild flowers
tip: Walk up the Pactolus bed from the gold refinery excavation; the badland pinnacles above the stream are the landscape everyone photographs from the temple and hardly anyone walks into.
todo: Walk the Pactolus stream bed
Buy sultanas at a roadside stall
Byzantine shops along the ancient road
rev: A pleasant half-hour after the ruins rather than a destination; visitors note there is essentially one café, no signage for the gold refinery site and dogs around the vineyard tracks.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 east on the D300 via Salihli; the İzmir–Uşak train calls at Sart

name: Bin Tepe Tumuli
desc: A hundred and fifty Lydian burial mounds scattered across the ridge above Lake Marmara, the largest — Alyattes's tomb, father of Croesus — 355 metres across and climbable in ten minutes. From the top the whole plain of Sardis and the lake open out, and you can see the other mounds standing like a bombing range of grass humps.
season: Mar–May for green ridges and wild flowers; Oct is clear and cool
tip: Drive the dirt track to the Alyattes mound rather than trying to reach the smaller ones — the burial chamber under it is usually locked but the climb and the view are the point.
todo: Climb the Alyattes tumulus
Count the mounds across the ridge
Look down over Lake Marmara
rev: Landscape-minded visitors find the field of mounds genuinely strange and memorable; others report unmarked farm tracks, a locked chamber entrance and nothing to see up close but grass.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 to Salihli and 15 km north on farm roads toward Gölmarmara

name: Mount Sipylus (Spil Dağı)
desc: A 1,500-metre limestone wall rising straight out of Manisa, protected as a national park, with black pine forest, wild horses on the upper meadows and the endemic Manisa tulip that flowers red across the slopes each spring. The road climbs to picnic terraces where the whole Gediz plain lies below you.
season: Apr–May for the Manisa tulip and wild horses; Sep–Oct for clear plain views
tip: Go up in the last two hours of daylight for the plain view, and in April look for the endemic tulip on the open slopes above the picnic areas rather than in the forest.
todo: Manisa tulips in April
Wild horses on the high meadows
Sunset terrace over the Gediz plain
rev: Locals treat it as their weekend mountain and rate the tulips and the views; visitors flag heavy weekend picnic litter, an entry charge per car and forest roads closed after snowfall.
entry: Small national park vehicle fee — check locally
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min north-east to Manisa on the O-33; the park road starts in the city's southern edge

name: Weeping Rock (Niobe)
desc: A weathered rock face on the lower slope of Spil Dağı that, from the right angle, resolves into a seated woman's head with water seeping down it. This is the Niobe of the myth, turned to stone weeping for her fourteen children, and it is the same rock Pausanias described nearly two thousand years ago.
season: Nov–Apr, when the seep is actually running — it dries out completely in summer
tip: Stand at the marked viewpoint below and slightly to the side; from directly underneath it is just a cliff, and half the visitors leave without ever seeing the face.
todo: Find the angle where the face appears
Read the Pausanias passage on site
Continue up to the Akpınar Cybele relief
rev: Classicists enjoy standing where Pausanias stood, but plenty of visitors say it is an ordinary rock with a good story, hard to make out, and the surroundings have been built up around it.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min to Manisa; the rock is on the city's southern ring road at the foot of Spil Dağı

name: Muradiye Mosque, Manisa
desc: A late Sinan mosque of 1585 with İznik tiles at their peak and a carved marble minbar, built for Murad III when Manisa was the training ground for Ottoman crown princes. The attached medrese now holds the town museum. Down the hill, the Sultan Mosque is where the Mesir paste is thrown to the crowd each spring.
season: Year-round; the Mesir festival falls in late March
tip: Time it for the Mesir Macunu festival in March, when paste wrapped in paper is thrown from the Sultan Mosque minaret and the whole town tries to catch it.
todo: İznik tile panels in the prayer hall
Manisa Museum in the old medrese
Mesir paste thrown at the Sultan Mosque
rev: The tilework gets real praise from people who make the detour, though Manisa itself is usually described as a rebuilt modern town with the monuments marooned among concrete blocks.
entry: Mosque free · museum small fee, covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 50 min north-east on the O-33; İZBAN suburban trains run İzmir–Manisa

name: Kula Volcanic Geopark
desc: Around eighty cinder cones and black basalt flows spread across the plateau east of Manisa, the youngest only a few thousand years old. The ancients called it Katakekaumene, the burnt land. Divlit cone can be climbed in half an hour, and near Sindel are human footprints pressed into volcanic ash perhaps twelve thousand years ago.
season: Apr–May and Oct — the black rock radiates heat and July–Aug is brutal out there
tip: The fossil footprints are fenced and easy to drive past; get the geopark map from Kula's visitor office first, because none of the cones are signposted from the main road.
todo: Climb Divlit cinder cone
Prehistoric footprints in volcanic ash
Basalt canyon of the Gediz at Adala
rev: Geology travellers rate it the most accessible volcanic field in Türkiye; everyone else notes bad tracks, no facilities, almost no interpretation on the ground and cones that look like slag heaps up close.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h 15 east on the D300 via Salihli to Kula; a car is essential on the plateau

name: Kula Old Town
desc: Some seven hundred timber-framed Ottoman houses on narrow lanes, many with painted ceilings and cumba bays overhanging the street, built by a town that grew rich on carpets and tanning. Restoration is patchy, so you walk past a perfect façade and then a collapsed one. Kula carpets are still woven here.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau hits 40 °C in summer and freezes in January
tip: Walk the lanes around the Kurşunlu Mosque on a weekday morning when doors are open and someone will usually invite you in to see a painted ceiling.
todo: Painted ceilings in a restored konak
Kurşunlu Mosque and its quarter
Watch a Kula carpet being woven
rev: Those who like unrestored Ottoman towns find it more honest than Şirince or Safranbolu; others are put off by the number of derelict houses, few places to eat and almost no tourist infrastructure.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h 15 east on the D300; intercity coaches on the İzmir–Uşak route stop in Kula

name: Salihli
desc: The market town for the Sardis plain, surrounded by sultana vineyards and with thermal springs at Kurşunlu and Çamurhamamı where the water comes out around 60 °C into old domed bathhouses. September is harvest, when the whole town smells of drying grapes and the roadsides are covered in laid-out raisins.
season: Sep–Oct for the raisin harvest; Nov–Mar is the proper thermal season
tip: Use Salihli as your base for Sardis, Bin Tepe and Kula rather than staying in Manisa — it is closer to all three and the thermal hotels are cheap midweek.
todo: Soak at Kurşunlu thermal baths
Sultana harvest in September
Day-trip base for Sardis and Bin Tepe
rev: Travellers use it as a functional and cheap base with good thermal baths; nobody pretends the town itself is attractive, and the older hamams are described as basic and dated.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 1 h 45 east on the D300; the İzmir–Uşak train stops at Salihli several times daily

name: Alaşehir (Philadelphia)
desc: The last of the Seven Churches of Revelation, and the last Byzantine city in Anatolia to fall. What survives is three huge brick piers of the sixth-century Church of St John, standing in a residential back street with frescoes still faintly visible under the arches. The surrounding hills are solid vineyard.
season: Sep–Oct for the grape harvest; Apr–May for green hills — July and August are over 38 °C
tip: The church piers are in a side street off the main road with one small sign; ask for Beş Eyvanlı Kilise and a local will point you, because the maps app frequently sends people wrong.
todo: Brick piers of the Church of St John
Faded frescoes under the arches
Vineyards and the September harvest
rev: Pilgrims following the Seven Churches find it moving; independent travellers usually say there are twenty minutes of ruins in an unremarkable town and little else to justify the drive.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then 2 h east via Salihli on the D300; the İzmir–Denizli regional train also calls here

name: Demirci
desc: A highland town at 850 m in the far north of the province, cut off from the coast by pine ridges, known for hand-knotted Demirci carpets and for the coldest winters in Manisa. Old timber houses survive around the çarşı, there is a Byzantine castle on the hill, and the plateau above has springs and thin summer air.
season: May–Oct — the road over the ridges is snowbound in stretches from December to March
tip: Ask at the carpet cooperative rather than the shops on the main street; the co-op still has weavers working and will show you looms without a sales pitch.
todo: Hand-knotted carpets at the co-op
Castle hill above the old çarşı
Cool plateau springs in summer
rev: Visitors who get there value the genuinely untouristed feel and the carpet workshops, while noting the long winding approach road, minimal accommodation and shops that shut early.
onward: İzmir Adnan Menderes (ADB), then about 3 h north-east via Akhisar and Gördes; coaches run from Manisa and Akhisar
